7.3 When asked to explain the mechanism adopted to ensure harmonization of 
packaging and labelling requirements under the Legal Metrology framework with the 
nutritional labelling norms prescribed by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of 
India (FSSAI), the Department of Consumer Affairs (DoCA), in its reply, stated as 
under: 
“The packaging and labelling norms under the Legal Metrology (Packaged 
Commodities) Rules, 2011 and the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and 
Display) Regulations, 2020 have been harmonized to ensure regulatory 
clarity, ease of compliance and consumer protection. 
 The nutritional labelling norms, including declarations related to sugar, 
fat, energy and other nutrient values, are exclusively prescribed by the Food 
Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). The Legal Metrology does 
not regulate nutritional content or quality parameters.  The harmonized 
framework is as follows: 
(i) Declarations related to the name and address of the 
manufacturer/packer/importer, the month and year of manufacture, pre -
packing or import and the best before/use by da te are governed by FSSAI 
regulations. 
(ii) Declarations such as the country of origin (for imported products), common 
or generic name of the commodity, net quantity, retail sale price (MRP) 
(inclusive of all taxes), unit sale price and consumer care detail s fall under the 
Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules.  
(iii) Regarding the size of letters and numerals, for declarations like net 
quantity, MRP, expiry/ best before date (where applicable) and consumer care 
details, the provisions of Legal Metrology Rules apply. For all other 
declarations, including nutritional information, the FSSAI regulations apply.

 This delineation ensures that quantity assurance is addressed under 
the Legal Metrology, while quality and nutritional assurance is under th e 
domain of FSSAI. This coordination fosters greater transparency, enhances 
consumer confidence and aligns with best practices in packaged commodities 
regulation.”

11.1 In regard to the steps undertaken by the Department of Consumer Affairs 
(DoCA) to protect the health of infants and children, including the measures enforced 
against food companies violati ng sugar-related labeling or formulation standards, the 
DoCA provided the following written reply:  
“The Department of Consumer Affairs (DoCA), through its Legal Metrology 
Division, has implemented several regulatory measures to protect consumers, 
including infants and children, by ensuring transparency and accuracy in 
packaging and labelling of pre -packaged commodities. Under the Legal 
Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, all packaged products —
including baby food —shall display mandatory informatio n such as net quantity, 
maximum retail price (MRP) inclusive of all taxes, country of origin (for imported 
products), and consumer care details. These measures are intended to 
safeguard consumers from misleading practices and ensure that essential 
quantitative information is accessible and legible on packaging, including those 
sold via e-commerce platforms.  
           However, it is important to note that the regulation of sugar content and 
nutritional labelling in food products, including baby food, does not fall under the 
jurisdiction of DoCA. Instead, such matters are regulated exclusively by the 
Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), under the Food Safety 
and Standards Act, 2006. The FSSAI's Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020 
and the  Foods for Infant Nutrition Regulations, 2020 govern nutritional claims 
and formulation standards. For instance, the infant food regulation prohibits the 
addition of sucrose or fructose unless specifically needed and restricts their total 
to not exceed 20% of total carbohydrate content.  
           As sugar content and related nutritional aspects fall outside the scope of 
the Legal Metrology Act, 2009, DoCA has not taken enforcement action against 
food companies for flouting sugar -related labelling or formulation norms. These 
violations ar e dealt with by FSSAI, which has the authority to issue notices, 
impose penalties, recall products and ban deceptive advertisements. DoCA, 
however, maintains coordination with FSSAI to harmonize packaging and 
labelling standards —ensuring declarations like “Best Before” dates follow 
FSSAI guidelines, while quantity -related declarations remain under Legal 
Metrology.  

43 
 
           Although no dedicated task force has been formed by DoCA for sugar -
specific violations, its officers do inspect both retail and onlin e markets for 
compliance with quantitative labelling norms. Consumer complaints related to 
incorrect net quantity or price are handled by the Legal Metrology Officers of the 
State Governments who enforces the provisions of the Legal Metrology Act, 
2009 and Rules made thereunder. Thus, while DoCA’s efforts focus on ensuring 
packaging transparency and standardization, the responsibility for regulating 
sugar levels and nutritional quality in food products for infants and children rests 
entirely with FSSAI.”

12.4 When asked about the specific s teps taken to harmonize the roles of the Food

12.5  On being asked about the steps the Department has taken to delineate 
responsibilities, es tablish uniform enforcement protocols, and coordinate effectively

between the Union and State Governments in relation to food business regulation, 
the DoCA furnished the following response:  
“FSSAI has informed that the implementation and enforcement of th e Food 
Safety and Standards Act, 2006 is a shared responsibility between the Central 
and State Governments. While the Food Safety and Standards Authority of 
India (FSSAI), under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, is responsible 
for laying down scie nce-based standards and ensuring overall coordination, 
the State Food Safety Authorities are primarily responsible for enforcement at 
the field level.  
As per provisions of Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and  
Registration of Food Businesses) Regulatio ns, 2011, the FBOs have been 
bifurcated into Centrally Licensed FBOs (as per Schedule 1 of the regulation) 
and State Licensed FBOs (for commencing or carrying on food business, 
which are not covered under Schedule 1). The Centrally Licensed FBOs come 
under the jurisdictional control of the FSSAI and the state Licensed FBOs 
come under the jurisdictional control of the respective State/UTs.  
The enforcement authorities viz., Commissioner of Food Safety, Designated 
Officer & Food Safety Officers in the States/U Ts perform their duties under 
sec 29 of the FSS Act and perform regular inspection, monitoring, 
surveillance, and sampling at the food businesses to verify & ensure 
compliance to the statutory standards & requirements under the FSS Act 
2006, FSS Rules 2011  and Food Safety & Standards Regulations notified 
from 2011 till date. In case of any non -compliance, punitive measures by the 
States/UTs are taken against the defaulting food business operators following 
the procedures as per the provisions under the FSS Act 2006. 
Further, in order to ensure uniformity in the implementation of harmonized and 
effective food safety enforcement mechanisms across all states, the Food 
Authority coordinates with the State Food Safety Authority and has 
undertaken the following key measures: 
(i)  Clear procedures on inspection, sampling, testing, and to initiate the 
penalties & punishment under FSS Act 2006, FSS Rules 2011 and 
regulations, ensuring consistency in implementation across States/UTs by 
State Food Authorities through CAC meetings.   
(ii) Regular training programs by FSSAI are conducted for Food Safety 
Officers (FSOs), Designated Officers (DOs), and laboratory personnel to 
enhance their enforcement capabilities and ensure standardized practices.  

52 
 
(iii)  Digital platforms like the Food Safety Compliance System (FoSCoS) 
and the Indian Food Laboratory Network (INFoLNet) to facilitate real -time 
monitoring and data sharing among enforcement authorities.  
(iv)  Regular engagement with State Food Safety Commissioners through 
Central Advisory Committee meetings (held quarterly) for reviewing the status 
of enforcement machinery and proper implementation of food safety 
measures.  The Central Advisory Committee ensures close cooperation 
between the Food Authority and the enforcement ag encies and organisations 
operating in the field of food.  
To further streamline effective coordination between Central and State 
Authorities and avoid jurisdictional issues, FSSAI has laid down directions for 
clear jurisdictional control of Central and Stat e authorities over central and 
state licensed FBOs while taking into consideration the need for early and 
effective response in cases of the Food safety emergencies. Thus there is a 
clear demarcation of responsibilities and jurisdiction between State/UTs f ood 
Safety Authorities and FSSAI complemented with uniform enforcement 
protocols to ensure effective coordination between the Union and State 
Governments.”

PART – II 
OBSERVATIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
1.  The Committee note that in light of the indications presented by the 
Indian Council of Medical Research and dietary guidance issued by the World 
Health Organization, it is evident that excessive sugar intake from packaged 
infant foods poses significant lon g-term health risks, including dental caries, 
obesity, metabolic disorders, and other chronic diseases. The Committee 
strongly opine that as infant foods marketed in India are intended to 
complement breast milk for children between six months and two years  of age, 
ensuring their nutritional safety is critical and be paramount for the 
Government. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend  the Government  that, from an overall 
perspective, it is essential that the sugar content in various categories of 
infant food pr oducts—such as infant formula, cereal -based complementary 
foods, follow -up formula, and packaged traditional infant foods —be carefully 
regulated and aligned with recommended dietary limits. Further, strengthening 
monitoring mechanisms, ensuring adherence t o nutritional guidelines, and 
promoting formulations with minimal or no added sugars would help protect 
infant health and support healthy growth and development.  
 
Mandatory Sugar-Level Classification for Packaged Foods  
2.  The Committee note that the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and 
Display) Regulations, 2020 mandate declaration of total sugar and added sugar 
content along with percentage contribution to Recommended Dietary 
Allowance (RDA), calculated on the basis of 2000 Kcal energy and 50 grams 
added sugar for an average adult per day.  
The Committee believe that while numerical disclosure of sugar and RDA 
percentages is scientifically accurate, many consumers may not easily 
interpret whether a product is high or low in sugar at the point of purchas e. 
Further, WHO’s recommended intake thresholds (10 per cent and 5 per cent of 

65 
 
total energy) differ from the 50 g adult RDA reference used for labelling 
purposes, which may lead to confusion.  
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommend introduction of a m andatory 
sugar-level classification framework under the Front -of-Pack Nutrition 
Labelling regime, based on clearly defined and scientifically derived 
thresholds aligned with WHO and Indian Council of Medical Research ( ICMR)– 
National Institute of Nutrition  (NIN) guidance, to facilitate immediate 
recognition by consumer.. 
 
Uniform Application of Sugar Labelling Norms Across Food Categories  
3.   The Committee note that sugar content varies across products 
depending on formulation, and prescribed existing regulations.  While the 
existing provisions under the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India’s 
Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020  mandate 
disclosure of total sugar and added sugar content on packaged food labels to 
facilitate informed consumer choice, the Committee feel that mere disclosure 
may not be sufficient to address the public health concerns arising from high 
sugar consumption. 
The Committee also observe that in the absence of uniform interpretive 
labelling nor ms across all food categories, consumers may receive 
inconsistent information, thereby limiting comparability and informed choice.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend the Government that in addition to 
strengthened labelling requirements such as enhanced v isibility of added 
sugar and related nutritional information, the possibility of prescribing specific 
limits for added sugar content in packaged food products, particularly those 
intended for infants and young children, be examined  and recommend that 
sugar disclosure and interpretive labelling requirements be uniformly applied 
across all packaged food categories without exemption, so that consumers 
receive consistent and comparable information irrespective of product type.  
The Committee are of view that establishing such limits would complement the 
existing labelling framework and further safeguard consumer health while 

66 
 
ensuring that food business operators progressively reformulate products to 
reduce excessive sugar content  
 
Explicit Declaration of Added Sugar in Foods Intended for Children  
4.  The Committee note that under Clause 3.6 of the Food Safety and 
Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, lactose and glucose 
polymers are the preferred carbohydrates for infant nutrition, and sucrose  
and/or fructose shall not exceed 20 per cent of total carbohydrate. FSSAI has 
clarified that this 20 per cent carbohydrate threshold corresponds to 
approximately 13.25 grams (≈53 Kcal), which is equivalent to 10 per cent of the 
530 Kcal total daily energy  requirement for infants aged 0 –6 months as per 
ICMR–NIN RDA. 
The Committee observe that although the regulatory limit aligns with Codex 
and EU standards and has been technically explained in terms of energy 
equivalence, such scientific equivalence is not evident to consumer/caregivers 
at the time of purchase and percentage of carbohydrate does not translate 
intuitively into the real sugar intake of infants.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend  the Government that all foods intended 
for or marketed to infants and children, wherever added sugar is present in 
any form, mandatorily carry a clear and prominent front -of-pack declaration 
stating the presence of added sugar in grams per serving, along with its 
percentage contribution to the daily energy requir ement of the target age 
group and if need be, the requisite amendments may be carried out in the 
respective acts/rule/regulations.  
 
Consumer Awareness on Health Impacts of High Sugar Intake  
5.  The Committee note that the World Health Organization recommen ds 
reducing the intake of free sugars to less than 10 per cent of total energy 
intake for both adults and children, and suggests that a further reduction 
below 5 per cent may provide additional health benefits. The Indian Council of 
Medical Research (ICMR) , in its Dietary Guidelines, 2024, recommends limiting 

67 
 
sugar intake to 25 grams per day and further states that added sugar provides 
no nutritive value other than calories. Also, global research link high sugar 
intake in early childhood to increased risks of dental caries, obesity, metabolic 
dysfunction, altered gut microbiome composition, type 2 diabetes and 
hypertension later in life. 
The Committee believe that while existing regulatory frameworks prescribe 
disclosure norms and compositional standards, lo ng-term behavioural change 
requires informed consumers. In particular, parents and caregivers of infants 
and young children may not always understand the cumulative health 
implications of early exposure to high -sugar diets. 
The Committee, therefore, recomm end that the Government should intensify 
and recalibrate nationwide consumer awareness campaigns, including the 
“Eat Right” initiatives, to specifically communicate WHO’s 10 per cent and 5 
per cent energy benchmarks and the 25 g/day ICMR recommendation in 
simplified and relatable formats. The Committee further recommend targeted 
outreach through schools, anganwadis, maternity clinics and digital platforms 
be initiated to ensure informed dietary choices for children.  The awareness 
about sugar content can fur ther be increased by enhancing the spread and 
frequency of engaging campaigns, collaborating with stake holders and 
sharing information on social media.  
 
Periodic Scientific Review of Sugar Thresholds in Infant Nutrition  
6.  The Committee note that FSSAI has stated that it regularly examines 
new scientific evidence through its Scientific Panels and Scientific Committee. 
It has clarified that the present limit of 20 per cent carbohydrate from 
sucrose/fructose in infant foods are aligned with Codex and Europ ean Union 
provisions. 
The Committee observe that although current limits are aligned with 
international standards, scientific knowledge on infant nutrition is 
continuously evolving  and firmly believe that  in view of the increasing public 
health concerns re garding sugar consumption in early childhood, it is 

68 
 
important that regulatory standards remain dynamic and responsive to 
emerging scientific evidence.  
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommend that permissible limits of 
sugar in infant formula, follow -up formula and complementary foods be 
periodically and systematically reviewed preferably at intervals of two to three 
years, by the concerned scientific bodies of the Food Safety and Standards 
Authority of India. Standard Operating Procedure to be frame fo r this and Inter 
departmental Training camps can be organised to successful implementation 
of the same.  The Committee further recommend that the outcome of such 
reviews, along with any proposed regulatory revisions, be  made public in a 
timely manner to en sure transparency , strengthen public trust in food safety 
regulation, and encourage progressive reformulation of infant food products in 
line with the latest scientific evidence.  
 
Expedited Notification of Front -of-Pack Nutrition Labelling (FOPNL) 
Regulations 
7.  The Committee are dismayed to note that the draft Front -of-Pack 
Nutrition Labelling (FOPNL) regulations were notified on 13 September 2022 
and that more than 14,000 stakeholder comments have been received, which 
are presently under examination and wider consultation.  
The Committee observe that over two years have lapsed since the draft 
notification, and the continued delay in finalising the regulations has resulted 
in the absence of simplified and interpretative front -of-pack information , 
particularly in relation to sugar content. In the context of increasing 
consumption of packaged and ultra -processed food, timely availability of clear 
and easily understandable nutritional information assumes significant 
importance for enabling informed diet ary choices. 
The Committee further observe that the present labelling framework relies 
primarily on numerical disclosures such as grams and percentage of 
Recommended Dietary Allowance, which may not be readily understood by all 
consumer at the point of pur chase.  The absence of simple interpretative tools 

69 
 
such as warning labels or colour -coded indicatory limits the effectiveness of 
such disclosures in guiding consumer behaviour.  
The Committee are of the view that clear, prominent and interpretative front -of-
pack warnings, especially for products high in sugar, can serve as an effective 
consumer information tool by providing immediate and easily understandable 
guidance at the point of purchase.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend the  FSSAI to finalise and not ify the 
Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labelling regulations within a defined and time -bound 
framework. The front -of-pack nutrition labelling should provide accessible, at -
a-glance information to help consumers quickly and easily identify the 
nutritional status of a product . The Committee further recommend  that the 
notified regulations  incorporate simple, , clearly visible and interpretative 
labelling mechanisms, including colour -coded indicators  for sugar levels in all 
products, using a three -colour format (red,  yellow, and green) to denote high, 
medium, and low sugar levels, or appropriate warning labels for products high 
in sugar. The Committee may also be apprised regarding the status of the 
same.  
 
Strengthening Oversight of E-Commerce Listings and Digital Ma rketing 
8.  The Committee note that the Department of Consumer Affairs has 
clarified that the regulation of mislabelled packaged food products, including 
those sold through e -commerce platforms, falls primarily within the 
jurisdiction of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India under the 
Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The Committee further note that the 
Department enforces declaration -related provisions on pre -packaged 
commodities through the Legal Metrology Act, 2009 and the Legal Metrology  
(Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, while misleading advertisements are 
addressed by the Central Consumer Protection Authority under the Consumer 
Protection Act, 2019. 
The Committee observe that with the rapid expansion of e -commerce, the sale 
of packaged food products through online platforms has increased 

70 
 
significantly, which may pose challenges in ensuring accurate labelling, 
truthful product claims and effective regu latory oversight. The absence of a 
dedicated institutional mechanism for monitoring mislabelling of food 
products sold online could lead to gaps in enforcement and delay in 
addressing misleading or non-compliant product listings. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Department of Consumer 
Affairs, in coordination with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, 
State Food Safety Authorities and the Central Consumer Protection Authority, 
explore the establishment of a coordinated monitoring mec hanism or joint 
task framework to specifically address issues relating to mislabelling and 
misleading claims in packaged food products sold on e -commerce platforms. 
The Committee further recommend that mechanisms for timely detection, real -
time monitoring and prompt removal of misleading product listings be 
strengthened in collaboration with e -commerce platforms so as to ensure 
effective enforcement of labelling norms and enhanced consumer protection 
in the digital marketplace. 
 
Strengthening Independent Th ird-Party Scientific Substantiation of Sugar -
Related and Health Claims  
9.  The Committee note that under Section 7(2) of the Food Safety and 
Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018, nutrient function 
claims and other function claims may be mad e only when they are supported 
by relevant and current scientific evidence  It has further been stated that 
where a claimed health benefit is directly attributed to a product, such claim 
must be based on statistically significant results from well -designed human 
intervention studies conducted by or under guidance of established research 
institutions and published in peer -reviewed journals. In certain cases, 
particularly those involving reduction of disease risk claims,  prior approval 
from the Food Authority is required  
The Committee also note that the primary responsibility for maintaining 
scientific evidence and substantiating such claims currently rests with the 

71 
 
Food Business Operators, while regulatory authorities may call for and 
examine this evidence during inspections or regulatory review  
The Committee observe that while the existing framework mandates scientific 
substantiation, reliance predominantly on documentation maintained by the 
Food Business Operator may give rise to concerns regarding objectivi ty, 
especially in relation to sugar -related claims such as “no added sugar,” 
“natural sweetener,” or implied health benefits in products marketed to 
children. In the absence of structured independent verification, consumers 
may not be fully assured of the robustness and neutrality of the scientific 
basis underlying such claims.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend that FSSAI strengthen the framework 
for third -party scientific substantiation of sugar -related and health claims by 
prescribing mandatory independent validation, wherever such claims relate to 
health benefits, nutritional superiority, or sugar substitution. The Committee 
further recommend creation of an empanelled list of accredited independent 
scientific institutions authorised to review an d certify supporting evidence, 
and summary details of such certifications be made publicly accessible to 
enhance transparency and consumer confidence.  The Front of Label Pack can 
mention the accreditation to build consumer Confidence.  
 
Regulation and Enforcement of Sugar-Related Claims 
10.  The Committee note that the regulatory framework governing 
advertising, labelling and claims on food products is clearly laid down under 
the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, the Food Safety and Standards 
(Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018 and the Food Safety and 
Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020. These regulations 
prescribe specific conditions for claims such as “Low Sugar” and “Sugar 
Free” and require that all claims be truthful, unambiguous , meaningful and 
supported by scientific evidence. The Committee further note that penalties for 
misbranded food and misleading advertisements may extend up to ₹3 lakh and 
₹10 lakh respectively under Sections 52 and 53 of the Act, and that an 
Advertisement Monitoring Committee has been constituted by the Food Safety 

72 
 
and Standards Authority of India to scrutinize advertisements across media 
platforms, including e-commerce. 
The Committee also take note of the recent initiative of the Food Safety and 
Standards Authority of India to enable consumers to report misleading claims 
on packaged food products through digital platforms such as the Food Safety 
Connect application and the FoSCoS Portal. The Committee view this initiative 
as a positive step towards strengt hening participatory regulation by enabling 
consumers to directly submit evidence such as front -of-pack images, licence 
details and e -commerce links to facilitate enforcement action against non -
compliant Food Business Operators.  
 
The Committee view this as  an important extension of the existing 
enforcement architecture, as it introduces a participatory dimension to 
regulatory oversight by allowing consumers to submit front -of-pack images, 
licence details and e -commerce links to facilitate evidence -based act ion 
against non-compliant Food Business Operators.  
The Committee firmly believe that while the legal and institutional framework 
to curb misleading claims is already in place, the effectiveness of scrutiny 
mechanisms can be significantly enhanced when cons umers are enabled to 
act as active informants. This is particularly relevant in categories such as 
infant foods and products carrying sugar -related or health -related claims, 
where misleading representations can have serious public health 
consequences. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that the Food Safety and Standards 
Authority of India strengthen enforcement by introducing graded penalties for 
repeat violations, prescribing mandatory timelines for withdrawal or correction 
of non -compliant advertisements  and claims, and ensuring regular public 
disclosure of violations and enforcement actions related to misleading sugar -
related claims. The Committee further recommend that the consumer reporting 
mechanism through digital platforms be institutionalised withi n the broader 
regulatory monitoring framework, with provisions for time -bound examination 

73 
 
of complaints, integration of complaint data into risk -based inspections, and 
periodic publication of action taken reports.  
The Committee are of the view that such me asures would enhance deterrence, 
strengthen consumer participation, and improve transparency and 
accountability in the regulation of food labelling and advertising, particularly in 
sensitive product categories such as infant foods and products carrying 
sugar-related or health-related claims. 
 
Institutionalising Periodic Post -Approval Re -Verification of Product 
Formulations 
11.  The Committee note that verification of sugar content in food products 
is undertaken during inspections through evaluation of raw materials, 
ingredient composition, formulation records, label scrutiny and sample 
testing. It has further been stated that current analytical methods can 
determine total carbohydrate or total sugar content, but added sugars cannot 
be analytically distingui shed from naturally occurring sugars through 
chemical testing alone. Manufacturers are required to maintain records 
regarding added sugars, which may be examined by regulatory authorities 
during inspection. 
The Committee further note that routine surveilla nce, sampling and 
inspections are carried out across the country, and that enforcement action is 
initiated in cases of non -conformity. However, there is no structured 
framework mandating periodic re -verification of product formulations after 
initial approv al or licensing, particularly in cases where reformulation may 
occur over time. 
The Committee observe that in the absence of a formalised post -approval re -
verification mechanism, reformulation of products leading to incremental 
increases in sugar content o r changes in ingredient composition may not be 
detected in a timely manner, especially where such changes remain within 
declared label parameters but alter nutritional quality. This concern assumes 

74 
 
greater significance in the case of infant and child foods , where even marginal 
changes in sugar composition may have long -term health implications.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend that FSSAI to institutionalise a 
structured periodic or risk -based post -approval re -verification mechanism for 
packaged food prod ucts, particularly those intended for infants and children. 
Such re -verification may include scrutiny of formulation records, ingredient 
sourcing documentation, and targeted market sampling at defined intervals. 
The Committee further recommend that reformu lated products be subject to 
mandatory re-declaration and, where applicable, prior regulatory intimation to 
ensure continued compliance with prescribed sugar standards.  
 
Enhanced Safeguards for Infant and Child Foods  
12.  The Committee note that during 2024–25, more than 4 lakh inspections 
were conducted across the country by State Governments and FSSAI Regional 
Offices, including approximately 1,100 inspections on units involved in foods 
for infants. Infant food businesses are categorised as high -risk under the Risk 
Based Inspection System (RBIS). Each Food Safety Officer has a monthly 
target of at least 10 inspections and 25 samples.  
The Committee observe that while inspection mechanisms are robust in 
aggregate terms, inspections specifically relating t o infant foods constitute a 
relatively small proportion of total inspections, despite infants representing 
the most vulnerable consumer group.  Further, they observe that infant and 
baby foods represent a uniquely sensitive category due to the vulnerability  of 
the target population. However, enforcement statistics relating specifically to 
infant food compliance are not presented in a distinct and consolidated annual 
format. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that infant and baby food products be 
accorded pr iority enforcement status, with a defined minimum percentage of 
annual inspections and sampling reserved for this segment. Compliance 
statistics relating specifically to infant and child foods should be reported 
separately in FSSAI’s Annual Report  detailing inspections conducted, samples 

75 
 
analysed, non -compliance rates, nature of violations (including sugar -related 
non-compliance), enforcement actions taken, and corrective steps 
implemented. This will ensure greater transparency and focused regulator y 
oversight in this critical segment.  
 
Strengthening Transparency and Inter-Agency Coordination 
13.  The Committee note that nutritional labelling and sugar regulation fall 
within FSSAI’s domain, while quantitative declarations such as net quantity 
and MRP fall under the Legal Metrology framework. It has been stated that no 
joint inspections on sugar content have been conducted due to allocation of 
business rules. 
The Committee observe that while statutory mandates are distinct, absence of 
structured coordi nation may lead to fragmented enforcement and regulatory 
gaps in cases involving misleading packaging.  
The Committee, therefore, recommend establishment of a structured 
coordination mechanism between FSSAI and the Department of Consumer 
Affairs for regular  information sharing, joint review meetings, and harmonised 
enforcement planning in matters involving nutritional disclosures and 
packaging practices. 
 
Strengthening Laboratory Infrastructure and Timely Testing  
14.  The Committee note that 243 NABL -accredited Primary Food 
Laboratories and 22 Referral Laboratories are notified under Section 43 of the 
FSS Act, 2006. Food Analysts are required under Section 46(3) to furnish 
reports within fourteen days. Additionally, 305 Mobile Food Testing 
Laboratories (Food Safety on Wheels) are deployed across 35 States/UTs.  
The Committee observe that keeping in view of the volume of inspections 
exceeding 4 lakh annually, laboratory capacity and turnaround time may face 
operational pressures, which could affect enforcement e fficiency. 

76 
 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that FSSAI undertake a comprehensive 
workload and capacity assessment of laboratories, publish State -wise average 
turnaround time statistics annually, and strengthen infrastructure and 
manpower in high -volume jurisdictions. They further suggest FSSAI to extend 
their horizon by including laboratory infrastructure of BIS and NTH.  
 
Disclosure of Average Laboratory Turnaround Time and Capacity Utilisation  
15.  The Committee note that. Under Section 46(3)of the FSS Act, 2006, Food 
Analysts are required to send analysis reports within fourteen days from the 
date of receipt of sample. Further, 305 Mobile Food Testing Laboratories (Food 
Safety on Wheels) are operational across 35 States/UTs.  
The Committee observe that w hile statutory timelines are clearly prescribed, 
concerns have been expressed regarding delays in receipt of laboratory 
reports in certain instances. In view of the number of inspections conducted 
annually, timely analysis of samples is critical for effect ive enforcement, 
especially in cases involving infant foods and high -sugar products. 
The Committee, therefore, recommend that FSSAI publish State -wise data on 
average sample analysis turnaround time, laboratory capacity utilisation, and 
backlog status. Whe re the fourteen -day statutory timeline is not consistently 
adhered to, corrective measures including augmentation of manpower, 
equipment, or laboratory infrastructure should be undertaken on priority.  
 
Dedicated National Monitoring Programme on Sugar Compliance 
16.  The Committee note that the Department of Consumer Affairs, through 
the enforcement of the Legal Metrology Act, 2009 and the Legal Metrology 
(Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011, ensures transparency in packaging and 
labelling of pre -packaged commodities, in cluding baby food, by mandating 
declarations such as net quantity, maximum retail price, country of origin and 
consumer care details. The Committee further note that the regulation of sugar 
content, nutritional labelling and formulation standards in infant  food products 

77 
 
falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Food Safety and Standards 
Authority of India under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the 
relevant regulations governing infant nutrition and food labelling.  
While acknowledging the res pective mandates of the two authorities, the 
Committee are surprised to know that there is no dedicated task force has 
been formed for sugar -specific violations. They  are of the view that effective 
consumer protection —particularly in respect of food produc ts meant for 
infants and children —requires closer coordination between regulatory bodies 
responsible for packaging declarations and nutritional standards . The 
Committee, therefore, recommend that the Department of Consumer Affairs 
and the Food Safety and S tandards Authority of India further strengthen their 
coordination and information -sharing mechanisms so that violations relating 
to packaging, labelling and nutritional standards, including sugar -related 
claims in infant food products, are identified and a cted upon in a timely and 
coordinated manner. The Committee believe that such an integrated regulatory 
approach would enhance transparency, improve enforcement effectiveness 
and better safeguard the health and interests of infants and children.

1 
 
CHAPTER – I 
 
 
INTRODUCTORY 
 
 
The primary policy objective of the Department of Food & Public Distribution, 
one of the two Departments of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public 
Distribution is to ensure food security for the country through timely and efficient 
procurement and distribution of Foodgrains. 
 
1.2 The Standing Committee on Food, Consumer Affairs and Public Distribution 
selected the subject - ‘Modernisation of Public Distribution System: Strengthening 
Technical Data base ’ for examination and Report  during 2024 -25, which further 
continued during the term 2025 -26. Accordingly, briefing and oral evidence on the 
subject were held on 27.03.2025, 02.07.2025 and 19.09.2025. 
 
1.3 The Committee’s examination of the subject,  ‘Modernisation of Public 
Distribution System: Strengthening Technical Data base ’, include Scheme for 
Modernisation And Reforms through Technology (SMART) – PDS, Modernisation 
and Strengthening of Public Distribution System (PDS), Implementation, Monitoring 
& Evaluation of the Scheme , Fair Price Shops, Direct Benefit Scheme (DBT) and 
PDS in States – Case Study  of Bihar, Kerala, Meghalaya, Tamil Nadu and 
Telangana. In view of the same, the PDS System  - its modernization, 
implementation, monitoring and evaluation has been discussed in detailed in the 
successive paras of the Report.  
 
Evolution of Public Distribution System (PDS)in India  
  
1.4 The Public Distribution System (PDS) evolved as a system of management of 
scarcity through distribution of foodgrains at affordable prices. Over the years, PDS 
has become an important part of Government’s policy for management of food 
economy in the country. PDS is supplemental in nature and is not intended to make 
available the entire requirement of any of the commodities distributed under it to a 
household or a section of the society. 
 
PDS is operated under the joint responsibility of the Central and the State/UT 
Governments. The Central Government, through Food Corporation of India (FCI), 
has assumed the responsibility for procurement, storage, transportation and bulk 
allocation of food grains to the State Governments. The operational responsibility 
including allocation within the State, identification of eligible families, issue of Ration 
Cards, supervision of the functioning of Fair Price Shops (FPSs) etc., rest with the 
State Governments. Under the PDS, presently the commodities namely wheat, rice, 
sugar and kerosene are being allocated to the States/UTs for distribution. Some 
States/UTs also distribute additional items of mass consumption through the PDS 
outlets such as pulses, edible oils, iodized salt, spices, etc. 
  
 
 
 

2 
 
History of Public Distribution 
  
Public Distribution System in 1960s 
 
1.5 The public distribution of essential commodities was in existence in the 
country during the inter -war period. However, PDS, with its focus on distribution of 
foodgrains in urban scarcity areas, had emanated from the critical food shortage of 
1960s. PDS had substantially contributed to the containment of rise in food grain 
prices and ensured access of food to urban consumers. As the national agricultural 
production had grown in the aftermath of Green Revolution, the outreach of PDS 
was extended to tribal blocks and areas of high incidence of poverty in the 1970s 
and 1980s. 
  
Revamped Public Distribution System (RPDS) 
 
1.6 The Revamped Public Distribution System (RPDS) was launched in June, 
1992 with a view to strengthen and streamline the PDS as well as to improve its 
reach in the far -flung, hilly, remote and inaccessible areas where a substantial 
section of the poor live. It covered 1775 blocks wherein area specific programmes 
such as the Drought Prone Area Programme  (DPAP), Integrated Tribal Development 
Projects (ITDP), Desert Development Programme (DDP) were being implemented 
and in certain Designated Hill Areas (DHA) which were identified in consultation with 
State Governments for special focus. Food grains for distribution in RPDS areas 
were issued to the States at 50 paise below the Central Issue Price. The scale of 
issue was up to 20 kg per card. 
 
The RPDS included area approach for ensuring effective reach of the PDS 
commodities, their delivery by State Governments at the doorstep of FPSs in the 
identified areas, additional ration cards to the left -out families, infrastructure 
requirements like additional Fair Price Shops, storage capacity etc. and additional 
commodities such as tea, salt, pulses, soap, etc. for distribution through PDS outlets. 
 
  
Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) 
 
1.7 In June, 1997, the Government of India launched the Targeted Public 
Distribution System (TPDS) with focus on the poor. Under the PDS, States were 
required to formulate and implement foolproof arrangements for identification of the 
poor for delivery of foodgrains and for its distribution in a transparent and 
accountable manner at the FPS level. 
 
The scheme, when introduced, was intended to benefit about 6 crore poor 
families for whom a quantity of about 72 lakh tonnes of food grains was earmarked 
annually. The identification of the poor under the scheme was done by the States as 
per State-wise poverty estimates of the Planning Commission for 1993 -94 based on 
the methodology of the "Expert Group on estimation of proportion and number of 
poor” chaired by Late Prof Lakdawala. The allocation of food grains to the 
States/UTs was made on the basis of average consumption in the past i.e. average 
annual off-take of food grains under the PDS during the past ten years at the time of 
introduction of TPDS. 

3 
 
  
The quantum of food grains in excess of the requirement of Below Poverty 
Line (BPL) families was provided to the State as ‘transitory allocation’ for which a 
quantum of 103 lakh tonnes of food grains was earmarked annually. Over and above 
the TPDS allocation, additional allocation to States was also given. The transitory 
allocation was intended for continuation of benefit of subsidized food grains to the 
population Above the Poverty Line (APL) as any sudden withdrawal of benefits 
existing under PDS from them was not considered desirable. The transitory 
allocation was issued at prices, which were subsidized but were higher than the 
prices for the BPL quota of food grains. 
  
Keeping in view the consensus on increasing the allocation of food grains to 
BPL families, and to better target the food subsidy, Government of India increased 
the allocation to BPL families from 10 kg to 20 kg of food grains per family per month 
at 50% of the economic cost and allocation to APL families at economic cost w.e.f. 
1.4.2000. The allocation of APL families was retained at the same level as at the time 
of introduction of TPDS but the Central Issue Prices (CIPs) for APL were fixed at 
100% of economic cost from that date so that the entire consumer subsidy could be 
directed to the benefit of the BPL population. However, the CIPs fixed in July and 
December, 2000 for BPL & AAY respectively and in July, 2002 for APL were not 
revised upwards since then even though procurement cost have gone up 
considerably. 
  
The number of BPL families was increased w.e.f. 1.12.2000 by shifting the 
base to the population projections of the Registrar General as on 1.3.2000 instead of 
the earlier population projection of 1995. With this increase, the total number of BPL 
families came to 652.03 lakh as against 596.23 lakh families originally estimated 
when TPDS was introduced in June 1997. 
  
Under the TPDS, the end retail price was fixed by the States/UTs after taking 
into account the margin for wholesalers/ retailers, transportation charges, lev y of 
local taxes etc. The States were earlier requested to issue food-grains at a difference 
of not more than 50 paise per kg over and above the CIP for BPL families. However, 
since 2001, flexibility was given to States/UTs in the matter of fixing the retail issue 
prices by removing the restriction of 50 paise per kg over and above the CIP for 
distribution of food grains under TPDS. 
  
 
Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) 
 
1.8 AAY was a step in the direction of making TPDS aim at reducing hunger 
among the poorest segments of the BPL population. A National Sample Survey 
Exercise pointed towards the fact that about 5% of the total population in the country 
sleeps without two square meals a day. This section of the population could be called 
as "hungry”. In order to make TPDS more focused and targeted towards this 
category of population, the "Antyodaya Anna Yojana” (AAY) was launched in 
December, 2000 for one crore poorest of the poor families. 
 
AAY involved identification of one crore poorest of the poor families from 
amongst the number of BPL families covered under TPDS within the States and 

4 
 
providing them food grains at a highly subsidized rate of Rs.2/ - per kg. for wheat and 
Rs.3/- per kg for rice. The States/UTs were required to bear the distribution cost, 
including margin to dealers and retailers as well as the transportation cost. Thus, the 
entire food subsidy was passed on to the consumers under the scheme. 
  
The scale of issue that was initially 25 kg per family per month was increased 
to 35 kg per family per month with effect from 1st April 2002. 
   
 
 
 
  

5 
 
CHAPTER – II 
 
 
Modernisation and Strengthening of Public Distribution System (PDS)  
 
 
Major Reforms in Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS)  
 
The Department has introduced major reforms in the functioning of TPDS 
through its modernization. To bring transparency & efficiency in TPDS operations, 
the Department, in association with all States/ UTs has implemented a plan scheme 
on End-to-End Computerization of TPDS Operations upto March, 2020 and central 
sector scheme namely Integrated Management of PDS (IMPDS) in all States/UTs 
w.e.f. April, 2018 upto March, 2023. The Department is implementing a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) –“Scheme for Modernization and Reforms through 
technology in Public Distribution System (SMART -PDS)” in association with all 
States/UTs from April, 2023 to March, 2026. 
 
2.2 As part of activities under the computerization scheme, around 20.5 Crore 
ration cards covering around 80 Crore beneficiaries under the National Food 
Security Act, 2013 (NFSA) are completely digitized. The Supply Chain Management 
of food grains is computerized in 31 out of 33 States/  UTs (except the UTs of 
Chandigarh, Puducherry, and Lakshadweep). 
 
 Digitised ration cards databases of States/ U Ts are also being seeded with 
available Aadhaar numbers of beneficiaries, and so far, at the national level more 
than 99.8% of ration cards (at least one member) and more than 99.3% beneficiaries 
(persons) have been Aadhaar seeded. This has enabled the States/  UTs to identify 
and weed out ineligible ration cards and duplicate/ ineligible beneficiaries while 
continuously reducing the pilferage of highly subsidized foodgrains, thereby 
increasing the rightful targeting of beneficiaries and thus food subsidies. The 
Aadhaar seeding of beneficiaries with their Ration Cards is being done by the 
respective State/ UT. 
 
2.3 Leveraging the strong foundations of end to -end computerisation, FPS 
automation and Aadhaar seeding/ authentication, the Department has implemented 
the One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC) feature for nationwide portability of ration 
cards under NFSA. The national portability of ration cards under the ONORC feature 
has been seamlessly enabled in all 36 States/ UTs covering around 80 Crore 
beneficiaries (100% of the total NFSA population of the country). 
 
Further, as an outcome of the use of technology in TPDS operations since 
2013, i.e., digitization of ration cards/beneficiary databases, Aadhaar seeding, de -
duplication process, ineligible records, deaths, permanent migration of beneficiaries, 
etc. all States/U Ts have been able to weed -out a total of about 6. 77 crore ration 
cards between 2013 to 2025 (till Dec 2025), and are being able to achieve rightful 
targeting of beneficiaries against the quota thus released. 
 
 
 

6 
 
Strengthening TPDS 
 
2.4 On the issue of measures undertaken to strengthen TPDS, the Department of 
Food and Public Distribution, in its Annual Report 2025–26, stated that: 
 
“To eliminate leakages and to ensure that all eligible households are 
continuously receiving their entitled quota of subsidized foodgrains under 
PMGKAY , through TPDS, the following measures have been taken by th is 
Department:  
 
(a) End-to-End Computerization of Targeted Public Distribution 
System (TPDS) 
 
The modernization of TPDS operations has been taken up by the 
Department with the implementation of a scheme on ‘End -to-End 
Computerization of TPDS Operations’ in collaboration with all the 
States/UTs under the XII Five Year Plan (2012 -17). The validity of the 
scheme was up to March, 2020 only. The following are the major 
achievements under the scheme:  
 
(i) Digitization of ration cards/ beneficiaries’ data completed in all 
States/UTs. The details of around 20.5 Crore ration Cards 
covering around 80 Crore beneficiaries are available on 
transparency portals of States/UTs. 
(ii) Aadhaar seeding of ration cards – Seeding of Aadhaar numbers 
is completed with more than 99.8% ration cards (at least one 
member), whereas nearly 99.3% beneficiaries are also Aadhaar 
seeded at the national level. 
(iii) Online allocation of foodgrains upto FPS level – Implemented in 
all States/UTs except two Union territories of Chandigarh and 
Puducherry which have adopted the Direct Benefit transfer (DBT 
Cash transfers) scheme of NFSA. 
(iv) Computerization of Supply Chain Management – Implemented 
in 31 out of 33 States/UTs except for two Union territories of 
Chandigarh and Puducherry under DBT Cash transfers, and 
other U T of Lakshadweep (small island). Its implementation in 
Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur is expected to be completed in 
the current year. 
(v) Grievance redressal facilities and transparency portals – Online 
grievance redressal systems and tollfree helplines/call centres 
(1967/1800- series) available in all States/UTs. 
(vi) Automation of Fair Price Shops – About 99.8% i.e. 5.50 Lakh of 
a total of 5.51 Lakh FPSs in the country have operational 
electronic Point of Sale (ePoS) devices for transparent 
distribution of subsidised foodgrains. 
 
 
 
 
 

7 
 
(b) Integrated Management of Public Distribution System (IM-PDS) 
 
With an objective to sustain the computerized TPDS operations and to 
introduce new reforms, the Department has implemented another 
central sector scheme, namely ‘Integrated Management of Public 
Distribution System’ (IM PDS) in all States/U Ts w.e.f. April 2018. The 
validity of the IM -PDS scheme was extended up to 31st March 2023. 
This scheme aimed to implement nationwide portability of ration card 
holders/beneficiaries covered under NFSA and to empower 
beneficiaries to lift their entitled foodgrains from any FPS of their choice 
in the country by using their same/existing ration card with 
biometric/Aadhaar authentication on ePoS device. The scheme also 
included setting up of central data repository of all ration card data in 
the country, national de -duplication, data analytics, cross learning and 
sharing of best practices between States/UTs, etc. Collectively this lead 
to the implementation of the One Nation One Ration Card feature for all 
NFSA/PMGKAY ration card holders. 
 
One Nation One Ration Card feature:  Initially the facility of One 
Nation One Ration Card was started  as inter -state portability w.e.f. 
August 2019 in 4 States of Andhra Pradesh & Telangana and Gujarat & 
Maharashtra by the then Hon’ble Minister of Consumer Affairs, Food 
and Public Distribution; and in January 2020 the facility of national 
portability of ration cards was seamlessly started in 12 States. Since 
then, the One Nation One Ration Card feature has been seamlessly 
enabled in all 36 States/ U Ts. The migratory beneficiaries/ households 
are now able to lift their entitled foodgrains from any FPS of their 
choice, anywhere in the country using their existing/same ration cards. 
The ONORC feature also includes intra -state portability of ration cards. 
Since inception in August 2019, a total of more than 200 Crore 
portability transactions (including inter -state and intra -state 
transactions) for the distribution of NFSA/ PMGKAY foodgrains have 
been recorded in States/UTs under ONORC. 
 
(c) Scheme for Modernization and Reforms through Technology in 
Public Distribution System (SMART-PDS) 
 
The approved scheme was envisaged to be implemented from April, 
2023 to March 2026. The scheme aimed to not only introduce major 
technological reforms but also to strengthen the technology 
infrastructure in the Public Distribution System (PDS) by introducing a 
technology-driven transformative change in the entire PDS ecosystem 
covering NFSA and State schemes. The scheme will overcome State 
level technological  limitations of PDS operations with respect to I T 
Hardware, Software, and technical Manpower by intr oducing a unified 
system covering all aspects of PDS -related operations from logistics to 
distribution across all 36 States/UTs and will incorporate the latest 
technologies for system implementation and operations for fast and 
secure PDS transactions. The total outlay of the scheme is Rs. 349.9 
Crore on cost sharing basis with all States/UTs. Financial assistance is 

8 
 
provided to States/UTs for cloud services, I T support teams and 
command control centres. Currently, NIC is developing the 
application/solution Pan India and the 1st phase of the new System is 
being deployed across the country. The present module -wise status of 
implementation is as under: 
 
Procurement Module: Development completed; customizations done 
for Uttarakhand State.  
 
RCMS, FPS & Grievance Monitoring: RCMS deployed in 1 6 States; 
Grievance Module under development (Routing Gateway ready; testing 
with Anna Sahayata and integration with SMART PDS in progress) 
 
Supply Chain & Allocation:  Development completed and 
implemented in 22 States.  
 
Biometric-based Distribution System:  Development completed and 
implemented in 30 States.” 
 
Upgradation to new technology  
 
2.5 While explaining the issue of technological upgradation, the representative of 
the Department of Food and Public Distribution apprised the Committee that: 
 
“Traditional or Monolithic architecture has been used in PDS Applications 
developed so far by States/UTs which lack modularity and scalability. 
Considering continues changes in technology, it is essential to transform entire 
PDS IT ecosystem.  
 
Thus, there is a need:  
 
➢ To sustain & strengthen key technology elements for continuous online 
operations without interruptions or compromising their performance;

Anna Chakra - PDS Supply Chain Optimisation Tool 
 
2.15 Providing an overview of the ‘Anna Chakra’ – PDS Supply Chain Optimisation 
Tool, the Department of Food and Public Distribution submitted in their written 
replies: 
 
“Anna Chakra’, PDS Supply Chain Optimisation Tool, is a significant step 
towards modernising the Public Distribution System. The Public Distribution 
System has been optimised through the Anna Chakra initiative, executed with 
support of WFP and IIT Delhi. Anna Chakra enhances efficiency and saves 
costs by optimising delivery routes, reducing fuel consumption and logistics 
expenses. Aligned with global sustainability goals and our Hon’ble PM’s Gati 
Shakti initiative, Anna Chakra exemplifies technology to create a resilient food 
system with minimal transport emissions, thus lowering the carbon footprint.  
 
In the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS), State Governments 
manage the movement of food grains through various supply chain nodes, 
including procurement centers, mills, intermediary storage, warehouses, FPS, 
and FCI.  Traditionally, supply chain network planning was done manually, 
focusing on proximity and administrative ease, which lead to inefficiencies, 
under-utilization of resources, increasing costs and lead times.  
 
 A route optimisation assessment was conducted for 30 states in the pilot 
project, and the results show tremendous promise, with estimated cost 
savings of about Rs. 250 crores per annum and a reduction in the distance 
from FCI godowns to ration shops by 15 -50%. Operations Research was 
applied to enhance the efficiency of the TPDS supply chain.  By optimally 
utilizing and tagging existing nodes like warehouses and FPS shops, the 
technical team (WFP, IIT-Delhi) developed optimization models to identify the 
network with the lowest overall costs.  This optimization does not require 
changes in infrastructure locations or capacit y but uses a state -specific 
algorithm based on actual data such as geo tagged locations of all network 
points, actual road distances, contracted transportation rates, warehouse 
capacities and FPS allocations. 
 
This exercise covered 4.37 lakh Fair Price Shops and approximately 6,700 
warehouses involved in the PDS supply chain. In the second phase, the 
optimisation of the supply chain will extend from mandis to FCI warehouses, 
state warehouses, and rice mills. The interstate route optimisation tool has 
been developed for optimising the PDS movement between the states and is 
integrated with the FOIS (Freight Operations Information System) portal of the 
Railways through the Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP). A significant 
milestone in this effort is the integration of the optimisation tool with the PM 
Gati Shakti platform, which now houses geolocations of FPSs and 
warehouses across the states. 
 
Besides the optimisation, and savings in both time and monetary terms 
through streamlined delivery routes with reduced fuel consumption, it also 
provides environmental benefits of a lower carbon footprint due to transport -
related emissions.”

2.16 In the course of providing information on the route optimization assessment 
conducted across States/UTs and the achievements under the Anna Chakra PDS 
System, the Department of Food and Public Distribution furnished information: 
 
“Anna Chakra” PDS Supply Chain Optimization Tool:  
 
On 5th December 2024, the Department of Food & Public Distribution (DFPD) 
launched the “Anna Chakra” optimization tool to enhance the efficiency of the 
Public Distribution System (PDS) supply chain. Designed to strengthen one of 
the world’s largest food safety nets, serving over 81 crore vulnerable people, 
the tool aims to reduce carbon emissions, improve delivery efficiency, and 
generate significant cost savings. The PDS Supply Chain Optimization 
programme began in March 2023 and covers routes transporting 680 LMT of 
food grains annually. It is being implemented in collaboration with the 
Foundation for Innovation and Technology Transfer (FITT), IIT Delhi, and the 
United Nations World Food Programme (UNWFP).  
 
After one year of implementation, assessments across 30 states show 
promising results, with transportation cost savings estimated at Rs. 250 crore 
annually. As of August 2025, the results of 30 states have been shared. 
 
(i)       Enhanced Efficiency and Cost Savings 
The implementation of the system is expected to deliver substantial 
annual savings of approximately Rs. 250 crores for both Central and 
State Governments. By enabling a 15 –50% reduction in travel 
distances, the system not only cuts down operational costs but also 
achieves nearly a 30% reduction in carbon emissions. Furthermore, it 
optimizes the use of over 6,700 warehouses that collectively serve 
around 4.5 lakh Fair Price Shops across the country. These 
advancements contribute to shorter transit times and significantly 
improved delivery timeliness, ensuring the timely distribution of food 
grains. 
  
(ii) Advanced Route Optimization 
Using sophisticated algorithms rooted in Operations Research (OR) 
and Artificial Intelligence (AI), the system determines the most efficient 
transportation routes for food grain movement. This approach results in 
a 15 –50% reduction in transport distances, minimizing exposure to 
bottlenecks and logistical disruptions. Additionally, the technology 
supports dynamic re -routing, allowing for quick adjustments during 
emergencies or unforeseen logistical challenges, thereby enhancing 
overall responsiveness. 
  
(iii)     Transparency Enhancements 
The system introduces robust transparency mechanisms, including 
systematic tracking of warehouse utilization and real -time monitoring of 
stock movements. Geospatial mapping of warehouses and Fair Price 
Shops(FPS) further aids visibility across the supply chain. Integration 
with the Gati Shakti National Master Plan ensures the use of updated 

16 
 
road infrastructure, while the FOIS (Freight Operations Information 
System) platform provides live freight rate data, optimizing interstate 
rail movements and improving transparency in transportation cost 
estimation. 
  
(iv) Accountability Mechanisms 
A key feature of the system is its emphasis on data -driven decision -
making, replacing older, convenience -based routing methods. With 
performance tracking tools and defined operational metrics, authorities 
can continuously assess and improve efficiency. Monthly reports 
detailing savings and route acceptances are submitted to the central 
government, fostering a culture of accountability and continuous 
performance evaluation. 
  
(v) Data-Driven Decision Making 
The platform automates and standardizes many of the previously 
manual supply chain planning processes, thereby reducing human 
errors and procedural delays. It utilizes state -specific models and 
historical data for demand forecasting and capacity planning. This 
data-backed approach enables proactive decision -making and efficient 
resource allocation, ensuring smoother and more reliable supply chain 
operations. 
  
(vi) Environmental and Sustainability Impact 
By drastically reducing transportation distances and fuel consumption 
through optimized logistics, the system contributes to a meaningful 
reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. This not only lessens the 
overall carbon footprint but also aligns with broader environmental and 
sustainability goals, making food distribution more eco -friendly and 
responsible. 
  
(vii) Resilience in Distribution 
The optimized supply chain is designed to ensure rapid recovery and 
continuity during disruptions. By minimizing operational costs, delivery 
times, and travel distances, the system enhances resilience, allowing 
supplies to be restored swiftly during disasters or emergencies. This 
ensures that vulnerable populations continue to receive essential food 
supplies even under adverse conditions. 
 
(viii) Seamless Inter-Ministerial Coordination 
The Anna Chakra system benefits significantly from the PM Gati Shakti 
ecosystem, gaining access to standardized, real -time infrastructure 
datasets from various ministries, including those overseeing railways, 
roads, and warehouses. This integration automates previously manual 
planning processes, enhancing coordination and efficiency. Moreover, 
the system is linked with the Railways’ FOIS through the Unified 
Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP), enabling smooth interstate and 
multimodal movement within the Public Distribution System (PDS).”

4.17 The Committee observe that the National Food Security Act, 2013 
(NFSA) provides for coverage of upto 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban 
population, at the all-India level, for receiving free of cost foodgrains. Section 9 
of the NFSA provides that the percentage coverage under the Targeted Public 
Distribution System in rural and urban areas for each State shall be

estimates as per the ce nsus of which the relevant figures have been

CHAPTER – VI 
 
 
DIRECT BENEFIT TRANSFER (DBT) 
 
 
Direct Benefit Transfer - Cash Transfers of Food Subsidy  
 
The National Food Security Act (2013) provides for reforms in the TPDS 
including schemes such as Cash transfers for the provisioning of food entitlements. 
In pursuance of enabling provisions under section 12 of NFSA for cash transfer, the 
Government notified ‘Cash transfer of Food Subsidy Rule, 2015’ in August 2015. 
Direct Cash transfer in food was started in UTs of Chandigarh and Puducherry from 
the month of September 2015 and part of Dadra & Nagar Haveli from March 2016. In 
these UTs, NFSA is being implemented in cash transfer mode under which the cash 
equivalent of subsidy is being transferred directly into the Bank accounts of eligible 
households to enable them to purchase food grains from the open market.

6.4 On being asked about the technology-driven reforms, the Department of Food 
and Public Distribution in their written replies furnished information as under:  
 
“The country’s Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) is governed by the 
provisions of National Food Security Act, 2013 (NFSA) for the distribution of 
free/subsidized food grains to about 81 Crore population (as per Census 2011). 
Annually, more than 550 Lakh MT of food grains is being allocated by the 
Government of India for distribution to nearly 20 Crore ration card holders 
under NFSA through a network of around 5.43 Lakh Fair Price Shops (FPSs) 
supported by almost 9,000 Godowns/Depots/Intermediate godowns of 
States/UTs and FCI/CWC/SWCs spread all over the country. 
  
In the recent years, significant technology -driven reforms have been brought in 
the functioning of TPDS to bring transparency and efficiency in the end -to-end 
operations as summarized below: 
  
(a) All 20 crore ration cards covering more than 80 crore beneficiaries 
under NFSA have been completely digitized in all States/UTs; of these 
almost 99.8% ration cards and 98.9% beneficiaries are also Aadhaar 
seeded. 
(b) 5.41 Lakh (99.6%) of total 5.43 Lakh FPSs in the country are 
automated by installing electronic Point of Sale (e-PoS) devices. 
(c) Computerization of Supply Chain Management is implemented in 31 
out of 33 States/UTs except for two Union Territories of Chandigarh and 
Puducherry under DBT Cash transfers, and other UT of Lakshadweep. 
Its implementation in Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur is expected to be 
completed in the current year. 
(d) Online allocation of food grains up to FPS levels is implemented in all 
States/UTs except two Union Territories of Chandigarh and Puducherry 
which have adopted the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT Cash transfers) 
scheme under NFSA. 
(e) Online grievance redressal mechanism/toll -free helplines and 
transparency portals are set up in all States/UTs. 
  
Presently, more than 98% of monthly allocated food grains to States/UTs are 
being distributed through biometric/Aadhaar authenticated electronic 
transactions and all the details pertaining to above PDS operations and 
distribution of food grains are available on Central and States/UTs web-portals.”  
 
 
6.5 On the issue of challenges/constraints faced by the Department such as 
ageing server infrastructure, software upgradation needs, integration challenges, the 
Department of Food and Public Distribution in their written replies submitted that:  
 
“The incumbent PDS system is serving its purpose well. However, there was an 
imminent need to modernize the PDS for the following reasons: 
 
• Technology architecture modernization:  However, with the advent of 
significant advancements in technology it was imperative to revisit the 
technology architecture of PDS 

47 
 
 
• Heterogeneous technology landscape:  Although end -to-end 
computerization of TPDS is completed and implemented across all 
States/UTs, the uneven and varied implementation of various applications 
developed under the Public Distribution System poses a significant 
challenge for the Centre and State Governments to further enhance and 
maintain these applications. Different versions of each module are 
developed at various levels in different technologies. State policies also 
differ, making component integration difficult. Replacing or modifying these 
applications is a challenging process, and collecting data from these 
unintegrated systems for central monitoring is a tedious task that needs 
immediate attention. This situation has also led to data duplication, defying 
the principle of data integrity 
 
• Hyper scaling and Capacity on demand:  Introducing hyper scaling 
capabilities, to achieve elasticity in infrastructure provisioning as per surge 
in usage 
 
• Cyber Security:  Increasing the cyber security resilience to meet the

assessment of the DBT cash transfer model in these UTs vis -a-vis physical

Central Bank Digital Currency – Digital Food Coupons 
 
6.8 Under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY), free foodgrains 
are being provided to approximately 80 crore beneficiaries across the country, with an 
annual subsidy outlay of about ₹2.4 lakh crore. The Department of Food & Public 
Distribution (DFPD), as the nodal Ministry for implementation of PMGKAY , has examined 
the potential of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) with a view to further enhancing 
transparency, strengthening beneficiary empowerment, and improving efficiency in 
foodgrain distribution under the Scheme. The use of programmable CBDC tokens offers 
significant promise as a transformative instrument for subsidy delivery by enabling 
precise targeting of beneficiaries, ensuring scheme-specific utilization, and minimizing 
the risks of diversion or misuse. The Section -12 of the NFSA talks about reforms of 
introducing schemes, such as, cash transfer, food coupons, or other schemes, to the 
targeted beneficiaries in order to ensure their foodgrain entitlements specified in Chapter 
II, in such area and manner as may be prescribed by the Central Government. 
 
The Budget provided for the Food subsidy under PMGKAY will be utilized for the 
pilot of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) in the Public Distribution System (PDS). 
 
The digital rupee or e -rupee is a tokenised digital version of the Indian rupee, 
issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC). 
The introduction of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC – Digital Rupee) offers an 
opportunity to enhance the DBT ecosystem by providing a secure, instant, traceable, and 
programmable digital cash mechanism for PMGKAY beneficiaries, thereby enabling 
smoother fund flow and reducing friction in availing entitlements. Use of CBDC in food 
subsidy delivery offers the following advantages: 
 
• Transparency/auditability: Beneficiaries will be able to access clear information 
regarding their monthly entitlement, the quantity of foodgrains allocated, the 
subsidy value extended by the Government, the quantity lifted, and the balance 
due. 
• Convenience boost: The system will minimize transaction delays and improving 
ease of access. 

49 
 
• Purpose-bound usage: Subsidy spendable only on foodgrains at authorized FPSs 
or empaneled grocery stores (DBT). 
• Beneficiary empowerment: By providing full visibility of entitlements and 
transactions, the initiative reinforces the rights of beneficiaries and enables them 
to claim their foodgrain entitlement with confidence and dignity. 
• Leakage reduction: FPS allocation next month based on redeemed CBDC 
tokens; ensures foodgrain-only redemption. 
• Token programmability: Conditions/restrictions on usage; set validity for monthly 
distribution. 
• Instant transfers: Direct subsidy crediting, bypassing NEFT/RTGS/IMPS. 
 
6.9 The Department shared information about the implementation of CBDC and 
future roadmaps as under: 
 
“The Food, Civil Supplies, and Consumer Affairs Department, Gujarat has 
implemented the CBDC pilot project from 15th February, 2026 in the Sabarmati 
zone of Ahmedabad city as well as in five fair price shops each in the urban areas 
of Surat, Anand, and Valsad districts. Direct Cash Transfer in food was started in 
UTs of Chandigarh and Puducherry from the month of September 2015 and 
urban part of Dadra & Nagar Haveli from March, 2016. This Department is 
planning to launch CBDC pilot project in Puducherry, DNH & DD and Chandigarh 
by providing subsidy amount in the form of CBDC token instead of transferring 
money into their bank account. 
 
After successful rollout of CBDC in foodgrain distribution and DBT , real time 
transaction data will be available for monitoring the CBDC implementation and 
performing the predictive analysis.” 
 
 
6.10 The Committee note that under the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna 
Yojana (PMGKAY), foodgrains are being provided free of cost to nearly 80 
crore beneficiaries, involving a substantial annual subsidy outlay of about ₹2.4 
lakh crore. The Committee appreciate the initiative of the Department of Food 
& Public Distribution to pilot the use of Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC – 
Digital Rupee) as a mechanism for subsidy delivery in the Public Distribution 
System (PDS). The Committee observe that the programmable nature of CBDC 
tokens has significant potential to enhance transparency, improve targeting 
and reduce leakages in the distribution of food subsidies. The Committee, 
therefore, recommend the Department to expedite the phased expansion of the 
CBDC pilot, leveraging its features of instant transfers, auditability and 
restricted usage to improve efficiency in subsidy delivery. The Committee also 
emphasize the need to utilize real -time transaction data for monitoring and 
predictive analysis to ensure a more targeted, transparent and efficient 
foodgrain distribution system under PMGKAY. 
(Recommendation No. 12)

The Department of Food and Public Distribution in their Annual Report 2025 –

and the State Governments, where the Central Government has assumed the 
responsibility for procurement, storage, transportation and allocation of foodgrains to 
all States/UTs. The operational responsibility of allocation of foodgrains within 
State/UT, identification of eligible families under NFSA, issuance of ration cards, 
distribution of foodgrains through Fair Price Shop (FPS) and licensing and 
monitoring of FPSs, etc. rests with the respective State/ UT Governments. Under 
PDS, foodgrains, namely, Rice, Wheat and Coarse -grains are being distributed to 
eligible households. Some States/UTs also distribute additional items of mass 
consumption through the PDS outlets such as sugar, pulses, edible oil, iodized salt, 
spices, etc. 
 
7.2 The eligibility criteria for coverage under TPDS are such that vulnerable 
groups like beggars, female domestic workers, ragpickers, sanitation workers etc. 
get covered. The Department has issued instructions to States/UTs from time to time 
to make special efforts to ensure the identification and inclusion of the extremely 
poor and needy households under NFSA. Ration card deletion during annual 
verification drives, deletion of duplicate ration cards under TPDS by many 
States/UTs under PDS reforms including computerization, which provides scope for 
issuance of new ration cards to such left out genuine beneficiaries. All States/UTs 
were requested to ensure that all left -out and genuinely deserving people belonging 
to weaker sections are covered under NFSA from time to time. 
 
7.3 The development and deployment of SMART -PDS application was taken up 
by the NIC. The development of project started in October, 2024 is expected to 
rollout in phases across States and UTs from April, 2025 and will be fully deployed by 
31st October, 2025.  
 
Bihar, Meghalaya, Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Kerala have made 
commendable progress in digitising beneficiary records, rolling out EPOS devices 
and integrating supply chain and grievance redressal systems. At the same time, 
issues such as biometric authentication failures, connectivity issues in rural areas 
and pending grievances continue to require attention.
